A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same NPPR research and GMM-based estimator. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable, allowing reliable matching despite substantial reorganization.

before.justification: v1 reports original robustness experiments across three image datasets and four classifier architectures, including dependency and up-sampling ablations and learned-distribution visualizations.

after.justification: v2 reports original robustness experiments, including revised benchmark results and additional corruption, cross-radius, feature-extractor, computational-cost, and baseline comparisons.

M1.justification: v1 describes extracting features from the classifier being evaluated. v2 permits a separate feature extractor and evaluates cross-backbone pairings in Table 5, a limited adaptation. The MLP heads, GMM, Gumbel–Softmax relaxation, softplus margin loss, and bicubic perturbation mapping remain.

E1.justification: The three image-classification datasets remain CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Tiny ImageNet. However, v2 adds actual evaluation under salt-and-pepper noise, motion blur, brightness changes, and JPEG compression in Table 11, substantially broadening coverage beyond the original norm-bounded perturbation evaluations.

E2.justification: v2 adds Laplace-distribution PR and AutoAttack to the main comparison, alongside the retained Gaussian/Uniform PR and PGD/CW references. Table 10 additionally evaluates a one-step PGD weak adversary and Rice et al.'s intermediate-stress formulation at multiple stress levels.

E3.justification: The reported PGD reference changes from 20 steps in v1 to 3 steps in v2's main comparison and 10 in its radius comparison. New protocols include training/evaluation radius mismatches up to 32/255, PGD-10-trained classifiers, severity-1 corruptions, cross-backbone feature configurations, and 100/300/500-epoch subset experiments. These additions do not establish that all existing experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds analyses of radius mismatch, feature-extractor choice, fitting/inference cost, mixture capacity versus optimization duration, and corruption robustness under standard and adversarial training. Conversely, v1's NPPR/entropy learning curves and train-versus-test generalization-gap analysis are removed. Most learned-distribution visualizations are retained in the appendix.

E5.justification: The corresponding main comparisons, v1 Table 3 and v2 Table 1, both report means and parenthesized standard deviations over 10 runs. No new seed reporting, confidence intervals, or significance tests are introduced. Different standard-deviation values do not change the reporting practice.

E6.justification: Results are extensively replaced and extended. ResNet18/CIFAR-10 NPPR changes from 88.32 in v1 Table 3 to 76.29 in v2 Table 1, alongside changed clean accuracy and evaluation settings, so this is not an established same-setting gain. At K=7, joint dependence is lowest in v1 Table 1, whereas label dependence is lowest in v2 Table 2: 64.88 versus 76.27 for joint dependence. Numerous new outcomes are added, while training-set ablation scores disappear.

T1.justification: v2 corrects AR's definition and corresponding proof by complementing the worst-case binary error. It adds a Gumbel–Softmax approximation-error lemma, a nonconvex SGD convergence theorem with variance decomposition, and finite-GMM approximation bounds using total variation distance. These substantially extend the theory in Sections 4 and Appendices A.2/B. The earlier ordering propositions, including the measure-zero case in the appendix, remain.

C1.justification: The central NPPR metric, learned-distribution estimator, and relationship to AR/PR remain the main contributions. v2 adds convergence guarantees to the stated estimator contribution and an efficiency claim to the conclusion, while removing the abstract's quantified 'up to 40%' claim.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly distinguishes ideal non-parametric NPPR from its restricted finite-GMM approximation and discusses the resulting conservativeness/computation trade-off. It adds interpretations concerning radius mismatch, corruption sensitivity, alternative feature extractors, and estimator-fitting overhead, and reports VGG16 adversarial-training convergence failure. The previous train/test generalization-gap interpretation is removed.

D1.justification: v2 supplies explicit training/evaluation algorithms, documents filtering correctly classified samples and clean normalization, and adds complexity, training-time, and inference-time information. It replaces the promised post-review code release with a stated public implementation link and supplies settings for new comparisons. The core hyperparameter and software/hardware configuration remains largely unchanged.

R1.justification: v2 substantially broadens positioning through randomized/game-theoretic AR literature and Rice et al.'s intermediate-stress formulation. Section 2.1 and Appendix E.3 distinguish uncertainty about perturbation distributions from intermediate-severity evaluation and weak attacks. Several historical GMM references are removed; publication-year updates to retained PR works are not new research coverage.

P1.justification: v2 retitles the paper, rewrites substantial method and conclusion passages, and divides the method presentation into distribution optimization, algorithms, and convergence. It reorganizes the experimental narrative around ablations, benchmark comparisons, and cross-radius analysis, while moving distribution-visualization discussion into a restructured appendix.

P2.justification: v2 replaces the original perturbation-example figure with a conceptual diagram, expands Figure 2 to include AR, and simplifies Figure 3. Dependency diagrams move to the appendix; the original learning curves disappear while their distribution panels are reassembled as Figure 7. New tables and algorithm boxes are added, comparison columns expand, and the extended ablation table replaces train/test columns with radius columns.

improvement.justification: v2 improves reproducibility, clarifies the finite-GMM limitation, corrects AR's definition, and adds useful validation. However, its new exponential relaxation guarantee is not established by Appendix A.2's Eq. 69, which drops the random Gumbel terms when bounding the expected error. The retained claim that stronger dependency consistently lowers NPPR also conflicts with revised Table 2, where label dependence outperforms joint dependence. These gains and substantive new inconsistencies prevent a reliable net quality judgment.
